title: Content moderation: definition and examples
description: Content moderation is the review of user content against rules and the law. Definition, methods (pre, post, AI, human) and why it matters to media and brands.
short: Content moderation is the process of reviewing user-generated content (comments, posts, images, videos) and deciding whether to keep, hide, remove or restrict it, based on a platform's rules and the applicable law.
body: Content moderation covers every decision an organisation takes about content it did not write itself but hosts or displays: a comment under an article, a reply on a brand's Facebook page, a review on a marketplace, a message in a forum. The possible actions go from leaving the content as it is to hiding it, deleting it, limiting its visibility or sanctioning its author.

Moderation can happen before publication (pre-moderation), after publication (post-moderation) or only when someone reports a problem (reactive moderation). It can be done by people, by software, or by both together, which is what most teams end up doing once volumes grow.

For a news publisher, a brand or a public body, moderation is what keeps a comment space usable: insults, spam and scams drive away readers and customers, while over-moderation silences legitimate criticism and damages trust. In the European Union, the Digital Services Act also sets procedural obligations for hosting services, such as handling reports and explaining decisions.

title: Comment moderation: definition and best practices
description: Comment moderation means reviewing comments on websites and social networks to keep debate open and remove abuse. Definition, methods and practical examples.
short: Comment moderation is the review of comments posted under articles, videos or social media posts in order to remove or hide abuse, spam and illegal content while keeping legitimate opinions, including criticism, visible.
body: Comment moderation is the most common form of content moderation for organisations that are not platforms themselves. Comments arrive fast, in large numbers and often at night or on weekends, especially when a topic is sensitive or a post goes viral.

Example: a regional newspaper publishes an article about a local election. Within an hour, hundreds of comments appear. Most are opinions, some are sharp criticism of the newspaper, a few contain insults aimed at a candidate and two contain a link to a fake giveaway. Good comment moderation hides the insults and the scam links and leaves all the opinions, including the criticism.

The difficulty is to be fast and consistent without being heavy-handed. Readers notice when comments disappear without explanation, and they also leave when a thread becomes toxic. A written moderation policy and a clear distinction between hiding and deleting help a lot.

title: Pre-moderation: definition, pros and cons
description: Pre-moderation means every comment is reviewed before it is published. Definition, advantages, drawbacks and when to use it instead of post-moderation.
short: Pre-moderation is a moderation method in which user content is held back and reviewed before it becomes visible to the public; nothing is published until it has been approved.
body: With pre-moderation, each comment goes into a waiting queue. A moderator or an automated system approves it, rejects it or edits it before anyone else can read it. It is the most protective method, because abusive content never reaches the audience.

Example: a public body opens comments on a consultation page about a sensitive local project. To avoid insults against named officials appearing even for a few minutes, it chooses pre-moderation: comments appear only once checked.

The cost is speed and conversation. If approval takes hours, discussions die and users feel censored. Pre-moderation suits small volumes, high-risk topics or audiences that include minors. Elsewhere, many teams prefer post-moderation combined with fast automated filtering, which keeps conversations live while still catching clear violations within seconds.

title: Post-moderation: definition and examples
description: Post-moderation means comments are published at once and reviewed afterwards. Definition, how it works, its risks and how automation makes it faster.
short: Post-moderation is a moderation method in which user content is published immediately and reviewed afterwards; content that breaks the rules is hidden or removed once it has been detected.
body: Post-moderation keeps conversations fluid: users see their comment straight away, and moderators review the flow after the fact. It is the default on most social networks and on many news sites.

The main risk is the window between publication and review. On a brand's Instagram post, an insulting or scam comment that stays visible for three hours can be screenshotted, liked and answered. The shorter that window, the safer post-moderation is.

This is why post-moderation is usually combined with automation: software reviews each comment within seconds of its publication and hides the clear violations, while people handle the borderline cases. OpenModeration works this way, with doubtful cases handled by its own team, on Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, WordPress and websites connected through its API.

title: Reactive moderation: definition and limits
description: Reactive moderation means content is only reviewed when a user reports it. Definition, how it works, its limits and how it relates to DSA notice and action.
short: Reactive moderation is a moderation method in which content is reviewed only after a user, a trusted flagger or an authority reports it, rather than being checked systematically.
body: In reactive moderation, the community does the first filtering: readers click a report button, and only reported content reaches the moderators. It is cheap and respects freedom of expression, since nothing is reviewed without a reason.

Its limit is obvious: abusive content stays online until someone bothers to report it, and many users never do. On a small brand page, an insult may remain visible for days. Reports can also be abused, for example when a group mass-reports a comment it disagrees with.

Reactive moderation is still essential, because the Digital Services Act requires hosting services to offer a notice and action mechanism (Article 16) so that anyone can report illegal content. In practice, organisations combine reports with proactive automated review so they do not depend on users alone.

title: Automated moderation: definition and how it works
description: Automated moderation uses software to review content and act on it without a person. Definition, techniques from keyword lists to AI, risks and good practice.
short: Automated moderation is the use of software (keyword filters, rules, machine-learning or language models) to analyse user content and take or propose a moderation decision without a person reviewing each item.
body: The oldest form of automated moderation is the keyword list: any comment containing a banned word is blocked. It is simple but crude, since it misses insults written with spelling tricks and blocks innocent sentences that happen to contain a listed word. Modern systems use AI models that read the whole sentence and its context.

Example: a YouTube channel receives thousands of comments per video. An automated system hides spam links and clear insults within seconds, so the community manager only looks at the few dozen comments the system is unsure about.

Automation brings speed and consistency, but it makes errors (false positives and false negatives), and the Digital Services Act requires providers to say when automated means were used in a decision (Article 17). Good practice is to automate the clear cases, send the doubtful ones to people, and keep a reason for each decision.

OpenModeration automates moderation according to each client's rules, hides clear violations automatically, keeps criticism visible, and has doubtful cases handled by its own team. You see every decision and its reason in real time and can step in at any moment.

title: Hybrid moderation: AI and humans working together
description: Hybrid moderation combines automated review for clear cases with human moderators for doubtful ones. Definition, how to split the work and why it works best.
short: Hybrid moderation is a moderation model in which software handles clear-cut content automatically and people review the ambiguous or sensitive cases, so each decision is taken by whoever is best placed to take it.
body: Pure human moderation does not scale, and pure automation makes mistakes on irony, quotes, slang and context. Hybrid moderation splits the work: the machine handles volume and speed, people handle nuance and responsibility.

Example: under a brand's post announcing a price increase, the AI hides obvious insults and spam at once, leaves angry but legitimate complaints visible, and sends a comment that might be a veiled threat to a moderator, who decides in a few seconds with the full context.

For media, brands and public bodies, hybrid moderation is the way to be both fast and fair. It also fits the Digital Services Act, which expects contested decisions on online platforms to be reviewed under the supervision of qualified staff and not solely by automated means (Article 20).

OpenModeration is built on this model: clear violations are hidden automatically, criticism stays visible, and doubtful cases are handled by the OpenModeration team. You see every decision in real time in one console and can override it whenever you want.

title: Human-in-the-loop moderation: definition
description: Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews the decisions an automated system is unsure about. Definition, comment moderation examples and DSA context.
short: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) describes an automated system in which a person reviews, confirms or corrects some of the machine's decisions, typically the uncertain, sensitive or contested ones.
body: In moderation, human-in-the-loop means the AI does not have the last word on everything. Cases below a confidence threshold, or in sensitive categories such as threats or self-harm, are routed to a person, who sees the content, its context and the reason the system flagged it.
Example: a comment says a politician should be shot down at the next election. A keyword-based system might read a threat; a person immediately understands the figure of speech and leaves it visible.

Human review also matters legally and reputationally. The Digital Services Act requires online platforms to handle complaints against moderation decisions under the supervision of appropriately qualified staff, not solely by automated means (Article 20). At OpenModeration, doubtful cases and contested decisions are reviewed by our team, and you see every decision in real time in one console.

title: AI moderation: definition, uses and limits
description: AI moderation uses machine learning and language models to read user content in context. Definition, how it differs from keyword filters, and its limits.
short: AI moderation is the use of artificial intelligence models, such as classifiers and large language models, to understand user content in context and decide or suggest whether it breaks moderation rules.
body: Unlike keyword lists, AI models read a comment as a whole: they can tell the difference between an insult and a quote, between criticism and harassment, or between a joke among regulars and a threat. Large language models can also apply rules written in plain language, such as a brand's community guidelines.

Example: the comment 'this product is a total scam, I want my money back' is a complaint, not a scam. A good AI moderation system leaves it visible and may flag it to customer service, while hiding 'click here to claim your free iPhone' as spam.
AI still makes errors, can be inconsistent on edge cases and needs safeguards: clear rules, thresholds, human review of doubtful cases and a written reason for each decision.
OpenModeration uses its own moderation AI, adapted to each client's rules and use cases, and cross-checks delicate cases with other AI models. New models are plugged in as they come out.

title: LLM (large language model) in moderation: definition
description: A large language model (LLM) is an AI trained on vast amounts of text to understand language. Definition and how LLMs are used in content moderation.
short: A large language model (LLM) is an artificial intelligence model trained on very large amounts of text to understand and generate language; in moderation, it can read content in context and apply rules written in plain language.
body: LLMs are the technology behind conversational assistants. Their strength for moderation is understanding: they grasp irony, coded insults, context from the article being commented, and they can follow instructions such as 'criticism of our products is allowed, personal attacks on employees are not'.
Example: a commenter writes 'nice job as always' under a post about a delayed train. An LLM can recognise sarcasm and classify it as criticism, which should stay visible, rather than praise or abuse.

LLMs also have limits: they can be inconsistent from one run to another, be fooled by carefully crafted text, and their cost and speed vary. That is why serious moderation systems frame them with rules, thresholds, cross-checks between models and human review. OpenModeration's own moderation AI is cross-checked by other AI models on delicate cases, and new models are added as they come out.

title: Model arbitration: several AIs checking a decision
description: Model arbitration means several AI models cross-check a moderation decision on delicate cases. Definition, how it reduces errors and when humans take over.
short: Model arbitration is a technique in which several AI models analyse the same content and their verdicts are compared, so that a moderation decision on a delicate case does not rest on a single model's judgement.
body: Every AI model has blind spots. Asking a second or third model to review a borderline comment, and comparing their answers, catches many of those errors. When the models agree, confidence in the decision is higher; when they disagree, it is a strong signal that the case is ambiguous.

Example: a comment uses a word that is a slur in one context and a reclaimed term in another. The first model flags it as hate speech, the second reads it as neutral. Rather than picking one at random, the system treats the disagreement as doubt and sends the comment to a human moderator.

Arbitration is usually reserved for delicate cases, since running several models on every comment would be slow and costly. OpenModeration uses its own moderation AI and cross-checks delicate cases with other AI models; new models are plugged in as they come out, and cases that remain uncertain are handled by the OpenModeration team.

title: False positive in moderation: definition and examples
description: A false positive is acceptable content wrongly flagged or removed by moderation. Definition, examples, why it hurts trust and how to keep the rate low.
h1: What is a false positive in moderation?
short: In moderation, a false positive is legitimate content that is wrongly identified as breaking the rules and therefore hidden, removed or flagged when it should have stayed visible.
body: False positives are the visible side of over-moderation. A reader who sees their reasonable comment disappear feels censored, and may say so loudly elsewhere. For a news publisher or a public body, removing legitimate criticism is a reputational risk in itself.

Example: a keyword filter blocks the comment 'the Scunthorpe match was great' because the town's name contains a banned string. Another classic: a comment quoting an insult in order to condemn it is removed as if it were the insult itself.

Lowering false positives means using models that read context, setting thresholds carefully, sending doubtful cases to people and letting users contest decisions. OpenModeration keeps criticism visible, hides automatically only clear violations, and records a written reason for every decision so errors can be spotted and corrected.

title: False negative in moderation: definition and examples
description: A false negative is harmful content that moderation fails to detect and leaves online. Definition, examples, causes and how to reduce misses safely.
h1: What is a false negative in moderation?
short: In moderation, a false negative is content that breaks the rules but is not detected, so it stays visible when it should have been hidden or removed.
body: False negatives are the misses of a moderation system: the insult written with numbers instead of letters, the scam link hidden behind a URL shortener, the harassment that only makes sense if you know the previous ten comments.

Example: under a brand's giveaway post, a fake account copying the brand's name replies to every participant with 'you won, claim your prize here'. If moderation misses it, customers may hand over their bank details to a fraudster.

There is always a trade-off between false negatives and false positives: a stricter threshold catches more abuse but removes more legitimate content. The right balance depends on the audience and the risk, which is why moderation rules should be set per client and per use case, as OpenModeration does.

title: Confidence score in AI moderation: definition
description: A confidence score expresses how sure an AI model is that content breaks a rule. Definition, how it works with thresholds, and why it is not proof.
h1: What is a confidence score in moderation?
short: A confidence score is a value, often between 0 and 1, that indicates how certain an AI model is that a piece of content belongs to a category such as spam, insult or hate speech.
body: Moderation models rarely answer just yes or no. They output a score per category, and the system decides what to do with it: act automatically above a high score, send to a person in the middle, leave the content alone below a low score.

Example: a comment gets 0.97 for spam because it contains a known scam link, so it is hidden at once. Another gets 0.55 for harassment because it is a harsh reply in a heated thread; it goes to a moderator instead of being hidden automatically.

A confidence score is not a measure of truth: a model can be very confident and wrong, especially on content unlike what it has seen before. Scores are useful only with well-chosen thresholds, regular checks of the decisions and human review of the uncertain zone.

title: Moderation threshold: definition and how to set it
description: A moderation threshold is the score above which content is hidden or sent for review. Definition, examples, and the trade-off between errors.
short: A moderation threshold is the cut-off value applied to a model's confidence score that decides what happens to content: automatic action above it, human review or no action below it.
body: Thresholds turn scores into decisions. Many systems use two: a high one above which content is hidden automatically, and a lower one that defines the band of doubtful content sent to a person.

Example: a children's brand sets a very low threshold for insults, because its audience is young and its tolerance is minimal. A political news site sets a higher one, because heated debate is part of its purpose and it does not want to remove sharp but legitimate opinions.

Raising a threshold reduces false positives but increases false negatives, and the reverse. There is no universal right value: it depends on the audience, the category of content and the cost of each type of error. OpenModeration adapts moderation to each client's rules and use cases and has the doubtful zone handled by its own team, while you see every decision in real time.

title: Moderation policy and community guidelines: definition
description: A moderation policy, or community guidelines, sets out what is allowed in a comment space and what happens otherwise. Definition, contents and practical tips.
short: A moderation policy, often published as community guidelines or a comment charter, is the set of rules that defines what content is allowed in a space, what is not, and what action is taken when the rules are broken.
body: A good policy is short, concrete and public. It lists what is not allowed (insults, hate speech, harassment, spam, personal data, illegal content), says clearly what is allowed (criticism, disagreement, off-topic within limits), and explains the possible actions: hiding, deletion, ban, and how to contest a decision.

Example: a city council's policy states that criticism of municipal decisions is welcome, that personal attacks on staff and residents are hidden, and that comments containing someone's phone number or address are removed immediately.

The policy is also what moderators and AI systems apply. Under the Digital Services Act, intermediary services must describe in their terms and conditions any restrictions they impose on content, including the tools used and whether decisions are automated or human (Article 14). OpenModeration moderates according to the rules each client defines, and its written reasons refer to those rules.

title: Hate speech online: definition and examples
description: Hate speech attacks people for who they are, such as origin, religion, gender or sexual orientation. Definition, examples, legal context and moderation tips.
short: Hate speech is content that attacks, demeans or incites violence or discrimination against people because of a protected characteristic such as origin, religion, gender, sexual orientation or disability.
body: Hate speech differs from an ordinary insult because it targets a group, or a person as a member of a group. In many EU countries, some forms are criminal offences; EU law also requires member states to criminalise public incitement to violence or hatred based on race, colour, religion, descent or national or ethnic origin.

Example: under an article about refugees, a comment arguing that immigration policy should be stricter is an opinion. A comment calling a nationality vermin or calling for violence against them is hate speech and should be removed.

Hate speech is hard to moderate because it is often coded, ironic or hidden behind spelling tricks, and because the same word can be an insult or a quote. Media and public bodies are especially exposed, and leaving such content online damages both their reputation and the safety of the people targeted. OpenModeration's AI reads comments in context, and ambiguous cases are handled by the OpenModeration team.

title: Online harassment: definition and moderation
description: Online harassment is repeated or coordinated abuse aimed at one person. Definition, forms (insults, threats, doxxing, pile-ons), examples and moderation.
short: Online harassment is abusive behaviour directed at a specific person, often repeated or coordinated, that aims to intimidate, humiliate or silence them, through insults, threats, unwanted contact or exposure of personal information.
body: Harassment is defined less by a single message than by a pattern: the same user replying insultingly to every post of a journalist, dozens of accounts targeting one commenter, or threats sent after a public statement. It can include doxxing, sexualised comments and impersonation.

Example: a reporter publishes an investigation. Over the next days, the comment section and her social media posts fill up with messages mocking her appearance, questioning her private life and hinting at where she lives. Each comment alone may look borderline; together they are harassment.

For media, brands and public bodies, protecting staff and community members is both a duty of care and a condition for open debate. Effective moderation looks at context and repetition, hides the abuse quickly and escalates threats. OpenModeration hides clear violations automatically and doubtful cases, often the subtle ones, are handled by the OpenModeration team.

title: Toxicity in comments: definition and detection
description: Toxicity describes rude, disrespectful or hostile content likely to make people leave a discussion. Definition, examples, how it is detected and its limits.
h1: What is toxicity in online comments?
short: Toxicity is a broad label for rude, disrespectful or aggressive content likely to make other people leave a conversation, including insults, contempt, threats and personal attacks.
body: Toxicity is a common category in moderation models because it captures the tone of a message rather than a precise offence. It is useful for spotting threads that are degenerating, but it is a fuzzy notion: what one community finds normal banter, another finds offensive.
Example: 'this article is lazy and badly researched' is negative but not toxic: it criticises the work. 'The author is an idiot who should be fired' is toxic: it attacks the person.

Treating every toxic score as grounds for removal leads to over-moderation, especially of strong but legitimate criticism. A better approach defines which kinds of toxicity the space does not accept and keeps the rest visible. OpenModeration applies each client's own rules, keeps criticism visible and hides clear violations.

title: Spam in comments: definition and how to stop it
description: Spam is unsolicited, repetitive or promotional content posted in bulk, often by bots. Definition, examples in comment sections and how to filter it.
short: Spam is unsolicited content posted in bulk or repeatedly, usually to advertise, drive traffic or deceive, such as promotional links, copied messages and bot-generated comments.
body: Comment spam ranges from the harmless to the dangerous: repeated self-promotion, links to dubious shops, fake reviews, and bots posting the same message under hundreds of posts. It drowns real conversation and makes a page look abandoned.

Example: under every video on a YouTube channel, accounts with attractive profile pictures post 'check my profile' or a link to an adult site. Within a week, the comment section is unreadable for regular viewers.

Spam is one of the easiest categories to automate because it is repetitive and recognisable, but spammers adapt quickly, with misspellings, emojis and new link formats. OpenModeration hides clear spam automatically on websites, Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and WordPress, so community managers can focus on real people.

title: Scams in comments: definition and examples
description: A scam is content designed to trick people into giving money or data, such as fake giveaways or impersonation. Definition, examples and moderation tips.
h1: What is a scam in comment moderation?
short: In moderation, a scam is content designed to deceive people into handing over money, personal data or account access, for example fake giveaways, fake customer service accounts or too-good-to-be-true investment offers.
body: Scammers like comment sections because they borrow the credibility of the page they post on. A reply that seems to come from the brand, under the brand's own post, is far more convincing than a random email.

Example: a retailer runs a contest on Instagram. Accounts named after the retailer with a slight variation reply to participants: 'Congratulations, you won! Send us your card details to cover shipping.' Each hour these comments stay visible, more customers are exposed.

Scams harm the people tricked and the brand whose name is used, and they tend to spike around contests, sales and news events. They should be hidden fast, ideally automatically. OpenModeration hides clear violations such as scam comments automatically on Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, WordPress and websites.

title: Phishing links in comments: definition
description: A phishing link leads to a fake page built to steal passwords, card details or personal data. Definition, how it appears in comments and how to remove it.
short: A phishing link is a link to a fraudulent website that imitates a trusted service, such as a bank, delivery company or brand, in order to steal login details, payment information or personal data.
body: In comment sections, phishing links are often disguised: shortened URLs, lookalike domain names, or a message inviting readers to 'check your account status' or 'claim your refund'. They frequently appear in replies to complaints, posing as customer support.

Example: a customer complains under an airline's Facebook post about a cancelled flight. Minutes later, an account called 'Airline Help Desk' replies with a link to a fake refund form that asks for card details.

Because the damage is immediate and concrete, phishing links should be hidden as soon as they are detected, without waiting for a report. Automated moderation is well suited to this: OpenModeration hides clear violations automatically, which includes obvious scam and phishing comments, and keeps a reason for each decision in the activity log.

title: Doxxing: definition and how to moderate it
description: Doxxing is publishing someone's private information, such as an address or phone number, without consent. Definition, examples, risks and moderation.
short: Doxxing is the publication of a person's private or identifying information, such as home address, phone number, workplace or family details, without their consent, usually to intimidate or expose them to harassment.
body: Doxxing turns online hostility into a physical risk. It can be explicit, like posting an address, or indirect, like sharing a photo of someone's street with a 'nice house you have here'.

Example: during a heated debate under a local news article, a commenter posts the full name and workplace of another participant, with a call to 'go and tell him what we think'. The comment should be removed immediately and the case escalated.

Doxxing also involves personal data, so it raises GDPR issues for the organisation hosting it. Moderation rules should treat it as a priority category with immediate removal rather than hiding for later review. OpenModeration lets each client define such rules, and doubtful cases are handled by the OpenModeration team.

title: Disinformation: definition and moderation
description: Disinformation is false information spread deliberately to deceive. Definition, difference with misinformation, examples and how moderation responds.
short: Disinformation is false or misleading information that is created or shared deliberately to deceive, gain money or influence, whereas misinformation is false information shared without the intention to mislead.
body: Not all false content is illegal, and moderators are rarely in a position to establish the truth on every topic. For most organisations, the question is not 'is this true?' but 'does this break our rules?': for example, impersonating an official source, spreading fake health advice that endangers people, or coordinated campaigns.

Example: during a flood, comments under a city's Facebook post claim that the drinking water is poisoned and link to a fake official notice. The public body needs to hide the fake notice fast and publish a clear correction.

Heavy-handed removal of opinions labelled as disinformation can backfire and fuel distrust. A clear policy, a focus on behaviour (fake accounts, coordination, impersonation) and human review of sensitive cases work better. Very large online platforms also have specific risk assessment duties under the Digital Services Act.

title: Astroturfing: definition and examples
description: Astroturfing is a fake grassroots campaign in which an organised group poses as ordinary citizens or customers. Definition, examples and warning signs.
short: Astroturfing is the practice of creating the appearance of spontaneous, grassroots support or opposition, through fake accounts, paid posters or coordinated messages that hide who is really behind them.
body: The name comes from AstroTurf, a brand of artificial grass: fake grassroots. In comment sections, astroturfing shows up as waves of similar messages from new accounts, all pushing the same view, product or attack within a short time.

Example: a week before a municipal vote on a new development, dozens of comments praising the project appear under the city's posts, from accounts created recently, using near-identical sentences. Readers come away with a false impression of public opinion.

Astroturfing is hard to spot message by message; it is a pattern visible across accounts and over time. Moderation teams look for repeated wording, recent accounts and timing. Fake reviews and undisclosed paid endorsements can also break consumer protection rules.

title: Brigading: definition and how to respond
description: Brigading is a coordinated pile-on in which a group floods a page with comments, votes or reports. Definition, examples, warning signs and responses.
short: Brigading is a coordinated action in which a group of users, often organised from another community, descends on a page or post to flood it with comments, votes or reports in order to impose a view or target someone.
body: Brigading is usually organised elsewhere, in a forum, a group chat or by an influencer pointing followers to a target. The participants may be real people, which distinguishes it from bot spam, but their behaviour is coordinated rather than spontaneous.

Example: a brand publishes a post supporting a social cause. A community hostile to that cause shares the link, and within two hours the post receives a thousand comments, many of them insulting, plus mass reports against the brand's replies.

The warning signs are a sudden spike in volume, many accounts that have never interacted with the page, and repeated slogans. Automated moderation helps absorb the spike by hiding clear violations immediately, while leaving genuine disagreement visible and sending borderline comments to a person.

title: Raid (online): definition and examples
description: A raid is a sudden, organised invasion of a live chat, stream or comment section by an outside group. Definition, examples and how to protect a community.
h1: What is a raid in online communities?
short: A raid is a sudden, organised arrival of a large number of outside users in a comment section, live chat or stream, usually to disrupt it with spam, insults or shocking content.
body: Raids are close to brigading but shorter and more chaotic: the goal is often disruption for its own sake rather than pushing a view. They are common during live events, such as livestreams, live blogs or online consultations, where comments appear in real time.

Example: during a live video Q&A with a mayor, an online group coordinates to post the same offensive meme and insults hundreds of times in ten minutes, making the chat unusable for residents who came to ask questions.

The answer is speed: during a raid, human moderators alone cannot keep up. Automatic hiding of clear violations, temporary restrictions on new accounts and a clear plan for live events limit the damage. Afterwards, an activity log helps understand what happened and adjust the rules.

title: Troll (internet): definition and how to deal with it
description: A troll posts provocative or off-topic messages to annoy, derail or get a reaction. Definition, difference with a critic, examples and how to moderate.
short: A troll is a person who deliberately posts provocative, insulting or off-topic messages in order to provoke reactions, derail a conversation or annoy other participants.
body: Trolling is about intent: the troll is not trying to convince, but to get a reaction. Typical behaviour includes bad-faith questions, deliberate provocation, repeated off-topic posts and baiting other users into insults.

Example: under every post of a museum, the same account comments that culture is a waste of taxpayers' money, in slightly different words, and answers each reply with sarcasm. The first comment is an opinion; the tenth is trolling.

It is important not to confuse trolls with critics. A customer complaining loudly about a product is not a troll, and removing them looks like censorship. Moderation should target behaviour that breaks the rules (insults, spam, harassment) rather than opinions. OpenModeration keeps criticism visible and hides clear violations.

title: Shadowban: definition and DSA transparency
description: A shadowban hides or limits a user's content without telling them. Definition, examples, why it is controversial and what the Digital Services Act says.
short: A shadowban is a restriction in which a user's content is hidden from others or made less visible without the user being clearly informed, so they keep posting without realising nobody sees it.
body: Shadowbanning is attractive to moderators because it quietly neutralises spammers and trolls without provoking them. On social networks, the term is also used more loosely by users who believe their reach has been reduced without explanation.

Example: on a forum, a persistent spammer's posts remain visible to him but not to anyone else. On Facebook, hiding a comment produces a similar effect: the comment remains visible to its author and their friends, but not to other visitors.

The practice is controversial because it lacks transparency. Under the Digital Services Act, hosting services must give affected users a statement of reasons when they restrict the visibility of their content, including demotion, unless an exception applies (Article 17). Organisations should therefore be careful with silent restrictions and keep a record of why each decision was taken.

title: Hide vs delete a comment: what is the difference?
description: Hiding a comment makes it invisible to the public but keeps it; deleting removes it for good. The difference, when to use each, and platform examples.
h1: Hide or delete a comment: what is the difference?
short: Hiding a comment makes it invisible to the public while keeping it (and on Facebook, still visible to its author and their friends); deleting removes it permanently. Hiding is reversible, deleting is not.
body: Most platforms offer both actions. On Facebook, a hidden comment stays visible to the person who wrote it and their friends, so the author does not feel censored and is less likely to escalate. On Instagram, hiding is also available, as are filters that hide offensive comments automatically. Deletion removes the comment for everyone.

Example: under a brand's post, a comment with an insult is hidden: the thread stays clean and the decision can be reversed if it was a mistake. A comment containing someone's phone number is deleted, because keeping it, even hidden, makes no sense.

Hiding is the safer default for automated moderation, because errors can be undone. Deletion suits content that must not be kept at all, or that the organisation is required to remove. OpenModeration hides clear violations automatically, which keeps decisions reversible, and records a reason for each in the activity log.

title: Ban (moderation): definition, types and good practice
description: A ban prevents a user from posting or accessing a space, temporarily or permanently. Definition, types of bans, when to use them and what the DSA requires.
h1: What is a ban in moderation?
short: A ban is a sanction that prevents a user from posting, commenting or accessing a community, either for a limited period (temporary ban or suspension) or permanently.
body: Bans target authors rather than individual messages. They are used for repeat offenders, spam accounts, and serious violations such as threats or doxxing. Most platforms let page owners ban a user from their page, which blocks further comments.

Example: a user has had six comments hidden in a week for insulting other readers of a news site. Instead of hiding each new one, the moderation team applies a 30-day suspension and tells the user why.

Because a ban is a heavier measure, it calls for a clear rule, a warning where possible and a record of the reasons. For online platforms, the Digital Services Act provides for a statement of reasons when an account is suspended or terminated (Article 17) and the possibility to contest the decision through an internal complaint-handling system (Article 20).

title: Moderation appeal: definition and how it works
description: An appeal lets a user contest a moderation decision and ask for a review. Definition, how it works, examples and the link with DSA complaint handling.
short: An appeal is the process that lets a user contest a moderation decision, such as a removed comment or a suspended account, and have it reviewed, ideally by someone other than the system that took it.
body: Appeals correct errors and make moderation more legitimate. A user who can explain why their comment was misunderstood, and get it restored, is far less likely to accuse the organisation of censorship.

Example: a reader's comment quoting a slur in order to condemn it was hidden automatically. The reader contests the decision, a moderator reads the full thread and restores it. The case is noted, and the rule is adjusted to handle quotes better.

On online platforms, the Digital Services Act turns appeals into an obligation: users must be able to lodge a complaint electronically and free of charge, for at least six months after the decision, and complaints must be handled under the supervision of qualified staff, not solely by automated means (Article 20). At OpenModeration, contested decisions are reviewed by our team as one of its DSA building blocks, and you see each review in real time.

title: Digital Services Act (DSA): definition and key rules
description: The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the EU regulation on intermediary services and content moderation. Definition, who it covers, key obligations and articles.
h1: What is the Digital Services Act (DSA)?
short: The Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) is the European Union regulation that sets rules for intermediary services, including hosting services and online platforms, on handling illegal content, moderation transparency and users' rights.
body: The DSA has applied to all services in its scope since 17 February 2024. It replaces part of the e-Commerce Directive's framework and keeps the principle that hosts are not liable for content they are unaware of, while adding procedural duties on how they handle content.

Its obligations are layered: some apply to all intermediary services, more to hosting services, more again to online platforms, and the heaviest to very large online platforms and search engines with over 45 million average monthly active users in the EU. Key articles for moderation include notice and action (Article 16), statement of reasons (Article 17), internal complaint handling (Article 20), trusted flaggers (Article 22) and transparency reporting (Articles 15 and 24).

For a media site, a brand or a public body that hosts comments, the practical questions are: can people report illegal content easily, do we explain our decisions, can users contest them, and can we produce figures on our moderation? Whether each obligation applies depends on the service and its size.

OpenModeration provides DSA building blocks: handling of reports, a statement of reasons for decisions, human review of contested decisions and exportable figures, with hosting in the EU. Reports and contested decisions are handled by our team, and you follow everything in real time.

title: Notice and action (DSA Article 16): definition
description: Notice and action is the DSA mechanism that lets anyone report illegal content to a hosting service. Definition, the rules of Article 16 and an example.
h1: What is notice and action under the DSA?
short: Notice and action is the mechanism, set out in Article 16 of the Digital Services Act, by which hosting services must let any person or entity report content they consider illegal, and must then process those reports in a timely, diligent, non-arbitrary and objective manner.
body: The mechanism must be easy to access, user-friendly and available electronically. A notice should contain, in particular, an explanation of why the content is considered illegal, its exact location such as a URL, the name and email of the person reporting (with exceptions for certain offences) and a statement that the notice is made in good faith.

Once a notice is received, the provider sends a confirmation of receipt if contact details were given, takes a decision, and informs the reporter of that decision and of any redress available. It must also say if it used automated means to process or decide on the notice.

Example: a reader reports a comment under a news article that publicly accuses a named person of a crime. The report is logged, a moderator assesses it, the comment is removed, and both the reporter and the author are informed, the author through a statement of reasons.
At OpenModeration, reports are handled by our team, with a written reason for every decision and an activity log: you see each report and its outcome in real time and can step in whenever you want.

title: Statement of reasons (DSA): definition and examples
description: A statement of reasons tells a user why their content was removed or restricted (DSA Article 17). Definition, required contents and a concrete example.
h1: What is a statement of reasons?
short: A statement of reasons is the clear and specific explanation that a hosting service must give a user when it restricts their content or account, setting out what was decided, on what facts, on what legal or contractual ground and how to contest it (DSA Article 17).
body: Article 17 applies to restrictions such as removing content, disabling access, demoting it or otherwise limiting its visibility, suspending payments, and suspending or terminating the service or the account. The statement must be provided at the latest when the restriction is imposed.

It must include, among other things: what the decision entails and its scope; the facts and circumstances relied on, including whether it followed a notice; whether automated means were used; the legal ground if the content is considered illegal, or the contractual ground (the terms and conditions) otherwise; and the redress options available, such as internal complaints, out-of-court dispute settlement and courts.

Example: 'Your comment of 12 March under the article Budget 2025 was hidden because it contains a personal insult aimed at another reader, which our comment policy prohibits (section 2). This decision was proposed by an automated system and confirmed by a moderator. You can contest it within six months via this form.'
OpenModeration records a written reason for every moderation decision and provides statements of reasons as one of its DSA building blocks; you see every decision and its reason in real time.

title: Trusted flagger (DSA Article 22): definition
description: A trusted flagger is an entity recognised under the DSA whose reports online platforms must handle with priority. Definition, rules of Article 22, example.
short: A trusted flagger is an entity with particular expertise, awarded that status by the Digital Services Coordinator of its member state, whose notices of illegal content online platforms must process with priority and without undue delay (DSA Article 22).
body: Trusted flagger status is not granted to individuals. The entity must show expertise in detecting illegal content, independence from online platforms, and that it submits notices diligently, accurately and objectively. Trusted flaggers publish an annual report on the notices they submit, and the status can be suspended or revoked if they misuse it.

Example: an association fighting antisemitism, recognised as a trusted flagger in its country, reports a comment on an online platform that it considers to be illegal incitement to hatred. The platform must treat this notice ahead of ordinary reports.

For organisations that host comments, the practical point is to identify notices coming from trusted flaggers and route them to the top of the moderation queue, with the same diligence and record-keeping as other reports.

title: Transparency report (DSA): definition and contents
description: A transparency report publishes figures on content moderation, as required by DSA Articles 15 and 24. Definition, typical contents and who must publish.
h1: What is a moderation transparency report?
short: A transparency report is a public document in which a service discloses figures and information about its content moderation, such as orders received, notices handled, decisions taken and complaints, as required by Articles 15 and 24 of the Digital Services Act.
body: Under Article 15, providers of intermediary services must publish, at least once a year, a clear report on their content moderation; micro and small enterprises are exempt unless they are very large online platforms. Article 24 adds information for online platforms, such as disputes submitted to out-of-court settlement bodies and suspensions, and requires them to publish their average monthly active users in the EU. Very large online platforms have to report more often.

Typical contents include: the number of notices received and the actions taken, the moderation carried out on the provider's own initiative, the use of automated tools, the number of complaints and their outcome, and median handling times.

Even when it is not mandatory, publishing figures on moderation reassures readers, customers and citizens that decisions are not arbitrary. OpenModeration provides exportable moderation figures and an activity log, which make such reports much easier to compile.

title: Internal complaint-handling system (DSA Article 20)
description: The internal complaint-handling system lets platform users contest moderation decisions (DSA Article 20). Definition, rules and a concrete example.
h1: What is an internal complaint-handling system?
short: An internal complaint-handling system is the process that online platforms must provide under Article 20 of the Digital Services Act so that users can contest, electronically and free of charge, decisions to remove or restrict their content or suspend their account.
body: Complaints must be possible for at least six months after the user is informed of the decision. The platform must handle them in a timely, non-discriminatory, diligent and non-arbitrary way, reverse the decision without undue delay if the complaint shows it was wrong, and inform the user of the outcome and of other redress options, such as out-of-court dispute settlement.

Crucially, decisions on complaints must be taken under the supervision of appropriately qualified staff and not solely on the basis of automated means. In other words, an AI can help, but a person must be accountable for the review.

Example: a user whose account was suspended for spam explains that he was posting links to his own local association. A moderator reviews his history, finds the suspension disproportionate, lifts it and replies with an explanation.
At OpenModeration, human review of contested decisions is one of the DSA building blocks: it is carried out by our team, and you see each complaint and its outcome in real time in the console.

title: Very large online platform (VLOP): DSA definition
description: A very large online platform (VLOP) has at least 45 million average monthly active users in the EU and is designated by the Commission (DSA Article 33).
h1: What is a very large online platform (VLOP)?
short: A very large online platform (VLOP) is an online platform with an average of at least 45 million monthly active recipients in the European Union that has been designated as such by the European Commission under Article 33 of the Digital Services Act.
body: VLOPs, together with very large online search engines (VLOSEs), carry the heaviest obligations of the DSA: assessing and mitigating systemic risks such as the spread of illegal content or effects on civic discourse, independent audits, data access for researchers and more frequent transparency reporting. They are supervised directly by the European Commission.

The 45 million threshold corresponds to roughly 10% of the EU population. Large social networks, marketplaces and app stores have been designated; a national news site or a brand's community space is far below it.

For most media, brands and public bodies, the VLOP regime does not apply to their own services, but it matters indirectly: when they moderate comments on Facebook, Instagram or YouTube, they work inside platforms that are themselves subject to it.

title: Hosting service (DSA): definition and obligations
description: A hosting service stores information provided by its users, such as comments. DSA definition, difference with an online platform and main obligations.
h1: What is a hosting service under the DSA?
short: Under the Digital Services Act, a hosting service is an intermediary service that stores information provided by, and at the request of, its users; an online platform is a hosting service that also disseminates that information to the public.
body: Hosting services benefit from a liability exemption: they are not liable for illegal content stored at a user's request as long as they have no actual knowledge of it and act expeditiously to remove it once they do. The DSA also imposes on them notice and action (Article 16) and statements of reasons (Article 17).

Online platforms, such as social networks or marketplaces, have additional duties, including the internal complaint-handling system (Article 20) and trusted flaggers (Article 22). The recitals of the DSA note that a comment section on an online newspaper can be a minor, ancillary feature that does not by itself make the newspaper an online platform; each case has to be assessed.

Example: a regional media group that runs its own comment system stores readers' comments on its servers. For those comments, it acts as a host and should be able to receive reports and explain its moderation decisions.
OpenModeration provides the DSA building blocks hosts typically need: report handling, statements of reasons, human review of contested decisions and exportable figures.

title: Illegal content (DSA): definition and examples
description: Illegal content is information that breaks EU law or a member state's law, as the DSA defines it. Definition, examples and difference with harmful content.
short: Under the Digital Services Act, illegal content is any information that, in itself or in relation to an activity, does not comply with EU law or the law of a member state; the DSA does not itself define what is illegal but refers to those laws.
body: What counts as illegal therefore varies between countries: defamation, incitement to hatred, threats, child sexual abuse material, terrorist content, the sale of counterfeit goods, copyright infringement and certain forms of harassment are common examples.

Illegal content is distinct from content that is legal but against a service's rules, such as rudeness, off-topic posts or spam. A host can remove both, but the legal ground differs: in a statement of reasons, it must say whether it relied on the law or on its own terms and conditions.

Example: a comment calling a minister incompetent is legal criticism. A comment falsely accusing a named local shopkeeper of theft may be defamatory, and a comment calling for violence against a religious group may be illegal incitement. The first stays; the others should be assessed and, if illegal, removed.
OpenModeration moderates according to each client's rules and records a written reason for each decision, which helps distinguish breaches of the law from breaches of the comment policy.

title: GDPR and content moderation: what to know
description: The GDPR is the EU regulation on personal data protection. Definition, and what it means for comment moderation: personal data, retention and hosting.
h1: What is the GDPR and how does it relate to moderation?
short: The General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) is the EU law, applicable since 25 May 2018, that governs the processing of personal data, including the names, messages and identifiers handled in comment moderation.
body: Moderating comments means processing personal data: usernames, profile information, the content of messages, sometimes IP addresses. The organisation must have a legal basis, inform users, limit retention to what is necessary and choose processors that offer sufficient guarantees.

Comments themselves can also contain personal data about third parties, such as a phone number, an address or health information. Removing doxxing quickly protects the people concerned and the organisation.
Example: a city uses a moderation tool for its Facebook page and its website. It lists the tool in its records of processing, signs a data processing agreement and checks where the data is hosted.
OpenModeration hosts its data in the EU, which simplifies the data protection analysis for European clients.

title: Audit trail in moderation: definition and uses
description: An audit trail, or activity log, records every moderation decision, who took it, when and why. Definition, why it matters for the DSA and examples of use.
h1: What is a moderation audit trail?
short: A moderation audit trail, or activity log, is a chronological record of moderation actions showing what was done to which content, when, by whom or by which system, and for what reason.
body: An audit trail answers the questions that come up after the fact: why was this comment hidden? Who restored it? Was the decision automated? Without it, a team cannot explain itself to a user, to management or to a regulator.

Example: a politician complains that his supporters' comments were removed from a news site's page. The editor checks the log: each comment was hidden for a stated reason, mostly spam links, two restored after review. The answer takes minutes.

Logs also feed DSA obligations: statements of reasons, complaint handling and transparency reports all rely on knowing what was decided and why. OpenModeration keeps an activity log and records a written reason for every decision, and moderation figures can be exported.

title: Trust and safety (T&S): definition
description: Trust and safety (T&S) protects users and an organisation from abuse, fraud and harmful content online. Definition, scope and its link with moderation.
short: Trust and safety (T&S) is the set of policies, teams and tools an organisation uses to protect its users and its service from abuse, fraud, harmful and illegal content, and to make sure people can rely on it.
body: The term comes from large online platforms, where trust and safety teams write policies, moderate content, fight fraud, handle law enforcement requests and respond to crises. Content moderation is one of its main activities, but T&S also covers product design, account security and regulatory compliance.
Example: a marketplace's trust and safety team removes fake listings, bans fraudulent sellers, moderates reviews and messages, and publishes the figures required by the Digital Services Act.

Media, brands and public bodies rarely have a dedicated T&S department, but they face the same questions on a smaller scale. With OpenModeration, you just connect your pages: automation and our team take care of the rest (doubtful cases, reports, contested decisions), and you see every decision and its reason in real time.

title: Content moderator: role, skills and challenges
description: A content moderator reviews user content and decides whether it complies with the rules. Definition, daily tasks, required skills and how AI changes the job.
h1: What does a content moderator do?
short: A content moderator is a person who reviews user-generated content, such as comments, posts and images, and decides whether it complies with a service's rules and the law, then takes or confirms the appropriate action.
body: Moderators apply the policy to real cases, many of them ambiguous: is this a joke or a threat, criticism or harassment, a quote or an insult? They need good judgement, knowledge of the community and the language, and consistency.

The job is demanding. Exposure to violent or hateful content takes a toll, and volume pressure leads to mistakes. Automation helps by taking the obvious cases off their hands, so that people spend their time on decisions that need judgement.

Example: a news site entrusts its comments to OpenModeration. The AI hides clear violations automatically, the few dozen doubtful cases are handled by the OpenModeration team, and the newsroom has nothing to do: it sees every decision and its reason in real time in the console and can take over at any moment. Moderation can also be fully outsourced.

title: Moderation queue: definition and how to manage it
description: A moderation queue is the list of content waiting for a human decision. Definition, how items enter it, how to prioritise it and how AI keeps it manageable.
short: A moderation queue is the list of content waiting for review by a moderator, such as comments held for approval, items flagged by the AI as doubtful, user reports and contested decisions.
body: The queue is where human moderation happens. It must be prioritised: a reported threat or a trusted flagger's notice comes before a borderline joke, and a contested decision with a deadline before routine checks.

Example: on Monday morning, a brand's community manager opens the console. Over the weekend, the AI hid 300 spam and insulting comments automatically and left the rest visible; the doubtful cases were handled by the OpenModeration team. She has no backlog to clear: she browses the decisions and their reasons, and can change any of them if she wants.

A queue that grows faster than it is processed is a sign the rules or thresholds need adjusting. With OpenModeration, the queue is not your job: clear violations are hidden automatically and doubtful cases are handled by our team, while you see everything in real time.

title: Sandbox mode in moderation: definition
description: Sandbox mode lets you test moderation rules on real content without acting on it. Definition, how it works, why it matters before going live, and an example.
h1: What is sandbox mode in moderation?
short: In moderation, sandbox mode is a test setting in which the system analyses real content and shows what it would decide, without actually hiding or removing anything.
body: Sandbox mode is how a team builds confidence before switching on automatic moderation. It shows which comments would be hidden, which would go to human review and why, so the rules and thresholds can be adjusted against the organisation's real audience.

Example: before automating moderation on its Facebook and Instagram pages, a retailer runs a sandbox for two weeks. It finds that complaints about delivery times would stay visible, as intended, but that a regional expression is wrongly treated as an insult, and corrects the rule.
OpenModeration offers a sandbox mode, so clients can see the decisions the system would take on their own comments before any action is applied.

title: Sentiment vs toxicity: what is the difference?
description: Sentiment says whether a comment is positive or negative; toxicity says whether it is abusive. Why confusing them leads to removing legitimate criticism.
h1: Sentiment vs toxicity: what is the difference?
short: Sentiment describes the emotional polarity of a message (positive, neutral or negative), while toxicity describes whether it is abusive; a negative comment is not necessarily toxic, and a toxic one can look positive.
body: Sentiment analysis is a marketing tool: it measures how people feel about a product, a campaign or an announcement. Toxicity detection is a moderation tool: it identifies insults, threats and attacks. The two are often confused, with harmful results.

Example: 'Your customer service is the worst I have ever dealt with, three weeks without an answer' is strongly negative but legitimate: it should stay visible and be answered. 'Great post, now go back to your country' sounds positive at first but is hateful.

Moderating on sentiment means removing criticism, which customers notice and which can turn a complaint into a public controversy. OpenModeration moderates on the client's rules, keeps criticism visible and hides clear violations.

title: Brand safety in comments: definition
description: Brand safety means protecting a brand from being associated with harmful content, including in its own comment sections. Definition, risks and examples.
short: Brand safety is the set of practices that protect a brand's reputation by preventing it from being associated with harmful, illegal or offensive content, whether in ads or in the comment sections of its own pages.
body: The term comes from advertising, where it means avoiding ads next to violent or extremist content. For a brand's social media pages, it also covers what appears under its own posts: a hateful comment left visible under a brand's post can be screenshotted and attributed to the brand's tolerance.
Example: a cosmetics brand's post with a model receives racist comments. If they stay visible for hours, the story becomes the brand's silence rather than the comments themselves.

Brand safety in comments relies on fast removal of clear violations, a published policy, and a team that answers legitimate complaints rather than hiding them. OpenModeration hides clear violations automatically on Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, WordPress and websites, and keeps criticism visible.

title: Community management: definition and role
description: Community management means animating, answering and moderating an online community for a brand, media or institution. Definition, tasks and moderation.
short: Community management is the work of building, animating and moderating an organisation's online community: publishing, answering comments and messages, handling complaints and enforcing the community's rules.
body: Community managers are the voice of the organisation on social networks and in comment spaces. Moderation is only part of their work, but it often takes the most time and stress, especially during a crisis or a viral post.

Example: a regional transport operator's community manager answers questions about delays, passes complaints to customer service, publishes service updates and deals with insults directed at drivers. On a strike day, comments increase tenfold.

Handing over moderation frees community managers for what only they can do: answering, explaining, defusing. With OpenModeration, clear violations are hidden automatically, doubtful cases are handled by our team and criticism stays visible so it can be answered; you see every decision in real time and can step in whenever you want.

title: UGC (user-generated content): definition
description: User-generated content (UGC) is content created by users rather than the organisation: comments, reviews, posts, photos. Definition, examples and moderation.
short: User-generated content (UGC) is any content created and published by users of a service rather than by the organisation itself, such as comments, reviews, forum posts, photos and videos.
body: UGC is valuable: comments create engagement, reviews drive sales and community posts bring authenticity. It is also a risk, because the organisation displays content it did not write and cannot fully control.

Example: a marketplace displays product reviews written by buyers, a news site shows readers' comments, and a city's participatory platform publishes residents' proposals. All three are UGC and all three need moderation rules.

Under the Digital Services Act, an organisation that stores UGC at users' request acts as a hosting service for that content, with obligations such as notice and action and statements of reasons. OpenModeration moderates UGC on websites through its API and on Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and WordPress.
